title: White musicians, Negro style and learning from Armstrong's records
summary: DeDroit says white players were influenced by Black musicians' style and that he copied Louis Armstrong's choruses and pacing, collecting his records.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: What was the question? I'm lost.

The question is, was there much attempt on part of white, legitimate musicians to play in a Negro style? Well there's no doubt that the white musicians who could play were influenced by their style. But to my positive knowledge, the Negro musicians didn't seem to have the schooling or the technique that the musicians had before they started to play jazz, you see? And that gave us a chance to perhaps improve or modernize in those days their style of music. But their music was always good. And I used to take a leaf out of Satchmo's book when I realized that he wasn't playing 32 bars in a whole number sometimes. And then I'd be out there blowing my head off and getting a tired lip, I found out how to distribute it. I learned, I learned. And the later years you'd notice that Louis Armstrong didn't play much more than 16 bars. He could play, but he wasn't bodily well. You know, Louis wasn't, and he's gone. And I'm frank enough to say that I didn't think it's wrong to copy some of his choruses. Because his clean style was the style that I liked. He didn't play that wild jazz. I had all these records, and Dutch Andrus, who had a little store on Oak Street, used to collect for me, all the Louis Armstrong records we could find, I gave them the lowest ten cents a piece. But I had a calamity, my granddaughter knocked them off the table and said, okay, okay. And I loved those records. I wouldn't have applauded with them at any price because his chorus only misbehaved and stuff like that, simply great. So there's no doubt that the colored musicians influenced the white musicians.
